title: History Writing
subtitle: Write about the past with distance, sourced evidence and honest debate

lessons.title: Le récit historique
lessons.description: Handle tenses, the historian's voice and narrative distance without slipping into anachronism.

blocks.heading: The tense system of historical narrative
blocks.body: Written history in French runs on a spine of passé simple for completed events that move the story forward, imparfait for background, states and habits, and plus-que-parfait for what came before. You are not expected to speak the passé simple, but at C1 you must read it fluently and recognise it instantly. A fourth option, the présent de narration, pulls a scene close to the reader — powerful, but used sparingly.

examples.french: Le conseil municipal vota la construction du pont en 1843.
examples.english: The town council voted for the construction of the bridge in 1843.
examples.note: passé simple: a single completed event

examples.french: La rivière débordait chaque printemps et emportait les passerelles de bois.
examples.english: The river overflowed every spring and carried away the wooden footbridges.

examples.french: Deux projets avaient déjà été rejetés lorsque l'ingénieur Vasseur présenta le sien.
examples.english: Two projects had already been rejected when the engineer Vasseur presented his own.

examples.french: Nous sommes en mars 1843 : la ville hésite encore.
examples.english: It is March 1843: the town is still hesitating.

examples.french: Le pont fut inauguré trois ans plus tard, sans discours.
examples.english: The bridge was inaugurated three years later, without speeches.

blocks.tip: In a research article the passé simple dominates; in a museum caption or a documentary voice-over, the present tense is common. Choose one system and stay in it.

blocks.heading: The historian's voice
blocks.body: Academic French history is written in a restrained, third-person voice. The first person appears only to signal a methodological choice (« nous retiendrons ici… »), never to express feelings about the actors. Judgement is carried by evidence and by carefully hedged verbs, not by adjectives.

examples.french: Nous retiendrons ici la datation proposée par l'inventaire de 1901.
examples.english: We shall adopt here the dating proposed by the 1901 inventory.

examples.french: Tout porte à croire que la halle servait aussi de tribunal.
examples.english: Everything suggests that the covered market also served as a courthouse.

examples.french: Les registres laissent entendre une baisse des naissances, sans permettre de la chiffrer.
examples.english: The registers hint at a fall in births, without allowing it to be quantified.

examples.french: L'auteur se garde de tout jugement sur les motivations des notables.
examples.english: The author refrains from any judgement on the motivations of the local notables.

examples.french: Il serait imprudent de conclure à une décision concertée.
examples.english: It would be unwise to conclude that the decision was coordinated.

blocks.tip: Hedging verbs — sembler, paraître, suggérer, laisser supposer — are the historian's politeness. Overclaiming reads as amateurish in French academic prose.

blocks.heading: Distance, and the trap of anachronism
blocks.body: Narrative distance means resisting the urge to describe the past in the vocabulary and values of the present. An anachronism can be lexical (calling a village clerk a « manager »), conceptual (attributing modern motives to people who could not have held them), or moral (judging the eighteenth century by twenty-first-century standards). The cure is to name the period's own categories and to mark clearly when you are speaking as a modern analyst.

examples.french: Parler de « chômage » avant 1880 relève de l'anachronisme : la catégorie n'existait pas.
examples.english: Speaking of "unemployment" before 1880 is anachronistic: the category did not exist.

examples.french: Ce que nous appellerions aujourd'hui un bibliothécaire s'appelait alors « le garde des livres ».
examples.english: What we would call a librarian today was then called "the keeper of the books".

examples.french: En termes contemporains, on qualifierait cette pratique de comptabilité analytique.
examples.english: In contemporary terms, one would describe this practice as cost accounting.
examples.note: the modern label is flagged as modern

examples.french: Les habitants ne pouvaient évidemment pas anticiper le tournant de 1870.
examples.english: The inhabitants obviously could not anticipate the turning point of 1870.

examples.french: L'historien évite de prêter aux acteurs une conscience qu'ils n'avaient pas.
examples.english: The historian avoids attributing to the actors an awareness they did not have.

blocks.tip: A useful test: could a person of the period have understood your sentence? If not, either rephrase it or announce it explicitly as your own analytical language.

items.example: Le récit historique n'est pas une simple liste de dates.
items.exampleEnglish: Historical narrative is not a mere list of dates.

items.example: La narration s'interrompt pour laisser place à une analyse.
items.exampleEnglish: The narration breaks off to make room for analysis.

items.example: Le narrateur reste discret et ne se met jamais en avant.
items.exampleEnglish: The narrator stays discreet and never puts himself forward.

items.example: L'historien signale toujours l'origine de ses informations.
items.exampleEnglish: The historian always indicates the origin of his information.

items.example: Le passé simple structure le récit écrit des faits achevés.
items.exampleEnglish: The passé simple structures the written account of completed events.

items.example: L'imparfait installe le décor avant l'événement.
items.exampleEnglish: The imperfect sets the scene before the event.

items.example: Le plus-que-parfait rappelle ce qui avait précédé la scène.
items.exampleEnglish: The pluperfect recalls what had preceded the scene.

items.example: Le présent de narration rapproche le lecteur de la scène.
items.exampleEnglish: The historic present brings the reader closer to the scene.

items.example: La distance du narrateur protège le lecteur de l'émotion facile.
items.exampleEnglish: The narrator's distance protects the reader from cheap emotion.

items.example: Il faut du recul pour interpréter un document si récent.
items.exampleEnglish: One needs detachment to interpret such a recent document.

items.example: Cet anachronisme fausse toute la démonstration.
items.exampleEnglish: This anachronism distorts the whole argument.

items.example: Le mot « rendement » est ici franchement anachronique.
items.exampleEnglish: The word "yield" is frankly anachronistic here.

items.example: La chronologie proposée en annexe reste provisoire.
items.exampleEnglish: The chronology proposed in the appendix remains provisional.

items.example: À l'époque, aucune loi n'imposait la conservation des registres.
items.exampleEnglish: At the time, no law required the preservation of registers.

items.example: Le document date du milieu du dix-huitième siècle.
items.exampleEnglish: The document dates from the middle of the eighteenth century.

items.example: Replacé dans son contexte, ce chiffre perd son caractère spectaculaire.
items.exampleEnglish: Put back into its context, this figure loses its spectacular character.

items.example: Cette lettre est contemporaine des travaux du canal.
items.exampleEnglish: This letter is contemporary with the canal works.

items.example: Une version antérieure du plan a été retrouvée en 1998.
items.exampleEnglish: An earlier version of the plan was found in 1998.

items.example: L'annotation en marge est postérieure d'au moins vingt ans.
items.exampleEnglish: The marginal annotation is at least twenty years later.

items.example: Ce témoignage tardif doit être manié avec prudence.
items.exampleEnglish: This late testimony must be handled with caution.

items.example: Le chroniqueur relate l'incendie sans jamais citer ses sources.
items.exampleEnglish: The chronicler recounts the fire without ever citing his sources.

items.example: L'auteur évoque brièvement la famine de 1817.
items.exampleEnglish: The author briefly mentions the famine of 1817.

items.example: Le rapport dépeint une ville tranquille, ce que démentent les registres.
items.exampleEnglish: The report depicts a quiet town, which the registers contradict.

items.example: La crue survint en pleine nuit, sans avertissement.
items.exampleEnglish: The flood occurred in the middle of the night, without warning.

items.example: Deux mauvaises récoltes ont précédé la révolte des tisserands.
items.exampleEnglish: Two bad harvests preceded the weavers' revolt.

items.example: Une longue période de calme succéda à ces troubles.
items.exampleEnglish: A long period of calm followed these disturbances.

items.english: the sequence, the chain of events
items.example: L'enchaînement des décisions apparaît clairement dans les minutes.
items.exampleEnglish: The chain of decisions appears clearly in the minutes.

items.example: La trame du chapitre suit les saisons agricoles.
items.exampleEnglish: The thread of the chapter follows the agricultural seasons.

items.example: Le déroulement exact de la séance nous échappe encore.
items.exampleEnglish: The exact course of the session still escapes us.

items.example: L'arrivée du chemin de fer constitue un tournant pour la vallée.
items.exampleEnglish: The arrival of the railway constitutes a turning point for the valley.

items.example: Parler de rupture serait excessif : les usages ont peu changé.
items.exampleEnglish: To speak of a break would be excessive: practices changed little.

items.example: L'étude insiste sur les continuités plutôt que sur les crises.
items.exampleEnglish: The study emphasises continuities rather than crises.

items.english: the point of view, the standpoint
items.example: Le point de vue adopté est celui des artisans, non des notables.
items.exampleEnglish: The standpoint adopted is that of the craftsmen, not of the notables.

items.example: L'objectivité totale est un idéal, non un état atteignable.
items.exampleEnglish: Total objectivity is an ideal, not an attainable state.

items.example: La neutralité du ton n'interdit pas la fermeté du raisonnement.
items.exampleEnglish: Neutrality of tone does not rule out firmness of reasoning.

items.example: Le style sobre de l'auteur donne du poids à ses conclusions.
items.exampleEnglish: The author's restrained style gives weight to his conclusions.

items.english: the pen; a writer's hand and style
items.example: On reconnaît sa plume à la sécheresse des transitions.
items.exampleEnglish: You recognise his pen by the dryness of the transitions.

items.example: Jadis, le marché se tenait sur le parvis de l'église.
items.exampleEnglish: In days gone by, the market was held on the church square.

blocks.heading: Recognising the passé simple
blocks.body: You need to decode the passé simple, not produce it. Regular -er verbs give -a / -èrent (il vota, ils votèrent); -ir and -re verbs give -it / -irent (il partit, ils partirent). The high-frequency irregulars are worth memorising as shapes: fut / furent (être), eut / eurent (avoir), fit / firent (faire), vint / vinrent (venir), put / purent (pouvoir), dut / durent (devoir).

examples.french: Le préfet ordonna la fermeture du moulin.
examples.english: The prefect ordered the closure of the mill.

examples.french: Les ouvriers refusèrent de signer le nouveau règlement.
examples.english: The workers refused to sign the new regulations.

examples.french: Elle mourut avant l'achèvement de son manuscrit.
examples.english: She died before the completion of her manuscript.

examples.french: Ce fut la dernière session tenue dans l'ancienne salle.
examples.english: That was the last session held in the old hall.

examples.french: Ils durent renoncer au projet faute de crédits.
examples.english: They had to give up the project for lack of funds.

examples.french: L'incendie détruisit la charpente mais épargna les archives.
examples.english: The fire destroyed the roof frame but spared the archives.

blocks.tip: Spoken and journalistic French replaces all of this with the passé composé. If you are unsure in your own writing, use the passé composé — it is never wrong, only less literary.

blocks.heading: Hedging and attributing: the modal toolkit
blocks.body: French historical prose signals the strength of a claim through verbs and impersonal structures rather than through adverbs like "maybe". Learn the ladder: il est établi que + indicative (certain), tout indique que + indicative (strong), il semble que + subjunctive (uncertain), il n'est pas exclu que + subjunctive (open possibility). Attribution uses selon, d'après, aux dires de.

examples.french: Il est établi que la halle existait déjà en 1720.
examples.english: It is established that the covered market already existed in 1720.

examples.french: Tout indique que le plan a été copié sur un modèle voisin.
examples.english: Everything indicates that the plan was copied from a neighbouring model.

examples.french: Il semble que le greffier ait antidaté l'acte.
examples.english: It seems the clerk backdated the deed.

examples.french: Il n'est pas exclu que deux mains différentes soient intervenues.
examples.english: It is not out of the question that two different hands were involved.

examples.french: Selon l'inventaire de 1901, le fonds comptait douze liasses.
examples.english: According to the 1901 inventory, the collection contained twelve bundles.

examples.french: D'après le curé, la cloche fut refondue deux fois.
examples.english: According to the parish priest, the bell was recast twice.

blocks.tip: « Il me semble que » takes the indicative, while « il semble que » alone takes the subjunctive. The personal version expresses your impression; the impersonal one expresses genuine doubt.

items.french: Le conseil vota la construction du pont, puis renonça faute de crédits.
options: The council voted for the construction of the bridge, then gave up for lack of funds.
The council refused the bridge and voted a new tax.
The council was building the bridge when the funds arrived.
The council will vote on the bridge once the funds are found.
items.answer: The council voted for the construction of the bridge, then gave up for lack of funds.

items.french: Il n'est pas exclu que deux mains différentes soient intervenues sur ce registre.
options: It is not out of the question that two different hands worked on this register.
It is certain that a single clerk wrote the whole register.
Two hands were forbidden to touch the register.
The register was rewritten by two later historians.

items.prompt: Present a cautious conclusion in a seminar.
items.tip: Link « porte à » smoothly and keep « croire » short; the whole phrase should sound like one calm unit, not four separate words.

items.french: Parler de « chômage » avant 1880 relèverait de l'anachronisme.
items.english: Speaking of "unemployment" before 1880 would be anachronistic.
items.prompt: Correct a colleague politely during a discussion.
items.tip: « Chômage » begins with a soft sh sound; keep the nasal in « anachronisme » light and let the final -isme end on a clear s-m.

items.french: L'arrivée du chemin de fer constitue un tournant pour toute la vallée.
items.english: The arrival of the railway constitutes a turning point for the whole valley.
items.prompt: Introduce the central claim of a talk.
items.tip: Stress falls on the last syllable of each group: arri-VÉE, chemin de FER, tour-NANT. Pause slightly before « pour toute la vallée ».

passages.title: Écrire le pont de Vaux-sur-Ance
passages.french:
Écrire l'histoire du pont de Vaux-sur-Ance oblige d'abord à choisir un temps.
Les plaques commémoratives du bourg emploient le présent : « En 1846, la ville se dote enfin d'un pont de pierre. »
Le ton est chaleureux, mais il efface toute distance entre le lecteur et l'événement.
La monographie de l'abbé Rieulx, publiée en 1889, préfère le passé simple : « Le conseil vota, l'ingénieur protesta, la crue emporta les échafaudages. »
Les verbes s'enchaînent, l'imparfait décrit le décor, et le récit avance sans que l'auteur se montre.
Cette sobriété n'est pas de la froideur : elle laisse aux documents le soin de convaincre.
Un troisième piège guette pourtant l'historien local, celui de l'anachronisme.
Lire les délibérations de 1843 comme un débat sur le « développement économique » revient à prêter aux conseillers un vocabulaire qu'ils n'avaient pas.
Leurs registres parlent de commodité, de sûreté, de la charge des ponts de bois emportés chaque printemps.
Ces mots-là ne sont pas de simples synonymes des nôtres : ils dessinent une autre manière de penser l'utilité publique.
L'historien peut évidemment traduire, à condition d'annoncer qu'il traduit.
« Ce que nous appellerions aujourd'hui un investissement public apparaît alors comme une dépense de sûreté » : la phrase est plus lourde, elle est aussi plus honnête.
Reste la question de la voix. L'abbé Rieulx écrivait « notre pont », et ce possessif engage un point de vue.
Une étude contemporaine écrira « le pont », quitte à préciser en note que l'auteur est né dans le bourg.
La neutralité complète n'existe pas ; la déclarer serait déjà une naïveté.
Mais le recul, lui, se travaille : il s'apprend dans le choix des temps, des mots et des silences.
passages.english:
Writing the history of the bridge at Vaux-sur-Ance first requires choosing a tense.
The commemorative plaques in the village use the present: "In 1846, the town at last acquires a stone bridge."
The tone is warm, but it erases all distance between the reader and the event.
Abbé Rieulx's monograph, published in 1889, prefers the passé simple: "The council voted, the engineer protested, the flood carried away the scaffolding."
The verbs follow one another, the imperfect describes the setting, and the narrative advances without the author showing himself.
This restraint is not coldness: it leaves the task of convincing to the documents.
A third trap, however, awaits the local historian: that of anachronism.
Reading the 1843 deliberations as a debate about "economic development" amounts to attributing to the councillors a vocabulary they did not have.
Their registers speak of convenience, of safety, of the burden of the wooden bridges carried away every spring.
Those words are not simple synonyms of ours: they sketch another way of thinking about public usefulness.
The historian may of course translate, provided he announces that he is translating.
"What we would today call a public investment appears at the time as an expenditure on safety": the sentence is heavier, it is also more honest.
There remains the question of voice. Abbé Rieulx wrote "our bridge", and that possessive commits him to a point of view.
A contemporary study will write "the bridge", even if it means specifying in a note that the author was born in the village.
Complete neutrality does not exist; to claim it would already be a naivety.
But detachment can be worked at: it is learned in the choice of tenses, of words and of silences.

lessons.title: Les sources et la critique
lessons.description: Examine a document's provenance, material form and content the way a trained researcher does.

blocks.heading: Critique externe: the document as an object
blocks.body: La critique externe asks whether a document is what it claims to be, before asking what it says. It examines the physical support — paper, parchment, ink, watermark, seal — the hand, the layout, the archival reference and the chain of custody. A perfectly sincere text on the wrong paper is still a problem.

examples.french: Le filigrane du papier renvoie à un moulin actif entre 1770 et 1795.
examples.english: The paper's watermark points to a mill active between 1770 and 1795.

examples.french: L'encre de la signature diffère nettement de celle du corps du texte.
examples.english: The ink of the signature differs markedly from that of the body of the text.

examples.french: Le sceau est intact, ce qui rend une substitution peu vraisemblable.
examples.english: The seal is intact, which makes a substitution unlikely.

examples.french: La pièce porte la cote 3 E 214, versée par la commune en 1953.
examples.english: The item bears the reference 3 E 214, deposited by the municipality in 1953.

examples.french: Il s'agit d'une copie du dix-neuvième siècle, non de l'original.
examples.english: This is a nineteenth-century copy, not the original.

blocks.tip: Always ask three questions of any archival item: who produced it, for whom, and how did it reach the shelf where you found it?

blocks.heading: Critique interne: what the text can and cannot say
blocks.body: La critique interne weighs the content: was the author in a position to know, did they have an interest in distorting, and does the text contradict itself or other sources? A reliable witness on one point may be worthless on another. Reliability is always assessed claim by claim, never granted to a document as a whole.

examples.french: Le greffier était présent à la séance : son témoignage est direct.
examples.english: The clerk was present at the session: his testimony is first-hand.

examples.french: En revanche, ce qu'il rapporte du marché voisin lui vient d'un tiers.
examples.english: On the other hand, what he reports about the neighbouring market comes to him from a third party.

examples.french: L'auteur avait un intérêt évident à minorer le nombre de journaliers.
examples.english: The author had an obvious interest in underreporting the number of day labourers.

examples.french: Les deux versions se contredisent sur la date, non sur les faits.
examples.english: The two versions contradict each other on the date, not on the facts.

examples.french: Ce chiffre, isolé, ne saurait être retenu sans corroboration.
examples.english: This figure, taken alone, cannot be accepted without corroboration.

blocks.tip: Distinguish sincérité (does the author believe what he writes?) from exactitude (is he right?). A completely sincere source can be completely mistaken.

blocks.heading: Cross-checking and admitting the gaps
blocks.body: Sound history recoupe: it lays independent sources side by side and reports where they agree, where they diverge and where nothing survives. Naming a lacuna is not a weakness of the study; concealing it is. The standard formula acknowledges the silence and stops there.

examples.french: Le cadastre et le registre paroissial concordent sur l'emplacement du four.
examples.english: The land register and the parish register agree on the location of the oven.

examples.french: Les comptes de 1802 à 1811 manquent : la série est lacunaire.
examples.english: The accounts from 1802 to 1811 are missing: the series has gaps.

examples.french: Aucune source ne permet de trancher entre les deux hypothèses.
examples.english: No source makes it possible to decide between the two hypotheses.

examples.french: Ces données sont corroborées par un inventaire indépendant de 1834.
examples.english: These data are corroborated by an independent inventory from 1834.

examples.french: Nous ignorons qui a rédigé la note en marge, et à quelle date.
examples.english: We do not know who wrote the marginal note, or on what date.

blocks.tip: « Nous ignorons… » and « les sources sont muettes sur… » are respectable sentences in French scholarship. Guessing to fill a hole is not.

items.example: Chaque affirmation doit reposer sur une source identifiable.
items.exampleEnglish: Every assertion must rest on an identifiable source.

items.example: La critique des sources précède toujours leur exploitation.
items.exampleEnglish: The critical examination of sources always precedes their use.

blocks.heading: The passive and the impersonal in method writing
blocks.body: Descriptions of archival work rely heavily on the passive and on se + verb, because the agent is either obvious or irrelevant. « Le fonds a été versé en 1953 » says what matters; who carried the boxes does not. The pronominal passive (« ce document se consulte sur place ») is lighter than the full passive and very common in institutional French.

examples.french: Le fonds a été versé aux archives départementales en 1953.
examples.english: The collection was deposited in the departmental archives in 1953.

examples.french: Ces registres se consultent uniquement sur microfilm.
examples.english: These registers may be consulted only on microfilm.

blocks.tip: French dislikes long passive chains. If two passives follow each other, turn one into « on + active » or a pronominal — the paragraph will breathe.

blocks.heading: Reporting doubt: conditionnel and concessive links
blocks.body: The conditionnel is the standard French device for a claim you are relaying without endorsing: « le document daterait de 1687 » means someone says so and you are not committing. Pair it with concessive connectors — quoique and bien que with the subjunctive, en dépit de and malgré with a noun, néanmoins and toutefois between clauses — to weigh conflicting evidence.

passages.title: La charte de la confrérie des tuiliers
passages.french:
Le fonds Berthaud, versé aux archives municipales de Craon-le-Haut en 1953, contient une pièce que trois générations d'érudits ont citée sans la discuter.
Il s'agit d'une charte accordant à la confrérie des tuiliers le droit d'extraire l'argile de la rive gauche, prétendument datée de 1687.
La critique externe suffit à faire naître le doute.
Le filigrane du papier renvoie à un moulin dont l'activité n'est attestée qu'à partir de 1804.
L'encre, uniforme d'un bout à l'autre, ne présente aucune des variations qu'entraîne normalement une rédaction étalée sur plusieurs séances.
Le sceau, enfin, est appliqué et non pendant, procédé inconnu dans la région avant le dix-neuvième siècle.
La critique interne conduit aux mêmes conclusions par un autre chemin.
La charte emploie le mot « propriétaire » dans un sens qui ne se généralise qu'après la Révolution.
Elle mentionne un pont que le cadastre situe à cinquante mètres de l'endroit indiqué, comme si l'auteur décrivait le paysage de son propre temps.
Surtout, elle règle avec une précision suspecte le point exact qui opposait la confrérie à la commune lors du procès de 1841.
Faut-il conclure à une falsification malveillante ? Rien ne l'impose.
La pièce peut être une reconstitution de bonne foi, rédigée pour remplacer un original perdu dont la teneur se transmettait oralement.
Les archives conservent d'ailleurs un brouillon anonyme, coté 2 J 17, dont la main ressemble à celle de la charte.
Nous ignorons qui l'a écrit, et l'inventaire de 1901 reste muet sur son entrée dans le fonds.
Ce faux, si c'en est un, n'en est pas moins une source excellente : il ne renseigne pas sur 1687, mais admirablement sur 1841.
passages.english:
The Berthaud collection, deposited in the municipal archives of Craon-le-Haut in 1953, contains an item that three generations of scholars have quoted without questioning it.
It is a charter granting the tilers' guild the right to extract clay from the left bank, allegedly dated 1687.
External criticism is enough to raise doubt.
The paper's watermark points to a mill whose activity is attested only from 1804 onwards.
The ink, uniform from beginning to end, shows none of the variations normally produced by a text written over several sittings.
The seal, finally, is applied rather than pendant, a technique unknown in the region before the nineteenth century.
Internal criticism leads to the same conclusions by another route.
The charter uses the word "owner" in a sense that becomes widespread only after the Revolution.
It mentions a bridge that the land register places fifty metres from the spot indicated, as if the author were describing the landscape of his own time.
Above all, it settles with suspicious precision the very point that set the guild against the municipality during the lawsuit of 1841.
Must we conclude that this was a malicious falsification? Nothing requires it.
The item may be a good-faith reconstruction, drawn up to replace a lost original whose content was passed on orally.
The archives also hold an anonymous draft, shelfmark 2 J 17, whose hand resembles that of the charter.
We do not know who wrote it, and the 1901 inventory is silent on how it entered the collection.
This forgery, if that is what it is, is nonetheless an excellent source: it tells us nothing about 1687, but a great deal about 1841.

lessons.title: L'historiographie
lessons.description: Follow how interpretations are proposed, contested and revised, and report a debate without taking sides.

blocks.heading: What historiography actually studies
blocks.body: Historiography does not study the past; it studies the writing of the past. Its objects are books, articles and the questions researchers thought worth asking. A historiographical paragraph therefore names people, dates of publication and schools of thought, exactly as an ordinary history names actors and events.

examples.french: L'historiographie de la métallurgie rurale a connu trois inflexions majeures.
examples.english: The historiography of rural metalworking has undergone three major shifts.

examples.french: Les travaux des années 1950 privilégiaient les séries de prix.
examples.english: The work of the 1950s gave priority to price series.

examples.french: Un courant plus récent s'intéresse aux gestes techniques eux-mêmes.
examples.english: A more recent current is interested in technical gestures themselves.

examples.french: La question de l'outillage n'a été posée qu'à partir de 1978.
examples.english: The question of tools was raised only from 1978 onwards.

examples.french: Ce déplacement de l'objet a renouvelé l'ensemble du dossier.
examples.english: This shift of object has renewed the whole file.

blocks.tip: A good historiographical review answers three questions: what did people ask, with what sources, and why did the question change?

blocks.heading: Reporting a debate without joining it
blocks.body: The standard French move is to attribute each position explicitly, present the strongest version of each, and only then say where you stand — or say that the state of the sources does not allow you to choose. Verbs of attribution (soutenir, avancer, objecter, nuancer) carry most of the work; adjectives of praise or blame carry none.

examples.french: Delaunay soutient que la fonderie fermait chaque hiver.
examples.english: Delaunay maintains that the foundry closed every winter.

examples.french: Marchand objecte que les livraisons de janvier contredisent cette lecture.
examples.english: Marchand objects that the January deliveries contradict this reading.

examples.french: Une troisième position, plus nuancée, distingue selon les décennies.
examples.english: A third position, more nuanced, draws distinctions by decade.

examples.french: Les deux thèses reposent sur le même fonds, lu différemment.
examples.english: Both theses rest on the same collection, read differently.

examples.french: En l'état des sources, la question demeure ouverte.
examples.english: Given the current state of the sources, the question remains open.

blocks.tip: Write the opposing thesis so well that its author would sign your summary. That is both good manners and the safest way to be taken seriously.

blocks.heading: Revision, and the apparatus that makes it possible
blocks.body: Interpretations are revised when new documents surface, when a method improves, or when a new question is asked of familiar material. Revision is ordinary scientific life, not scandal. It only works because of the apparatus: footnotes, references, bibliography and peer review let a reader retrace every step and disagree precisely.

examples.french: La découverte de deux liasses a imposé une révision de la chronologie.
examples.english: The discovery of two bundles has forced a revision of the chronology.

examples.french: Chaque affirmation renvoie en note à la cote exacte du document.
examples.english: Each assertion refers in a footnote to the exact shelfmark of the document.

examples.french: L'article a été soumis à la lecture de deux pairs anonymes.
examples.english: The article was submitted to two anonymous peer reviewers.

examples.french: Le compte rendu paru dans la revue signale une lacune bibliographique.
examples.english: The review published in the journal points out a bibliographical gap.

examples.french: Réviser une thèse n'est pas la désavouer : c'est la faire travailler.
examples.english: To revise a thesis is not to disown it: it is to put it to work.

blocks.tip: In French academic style the footnote is where you prove; the body text is where you argue. Keep proof out of your sentences and they will read far more cleanly.

blocks.heading: Attributing positions: verbs and their moods
blocks.body: Verbs of saying take the indicative when you simply relay a position (soutenir que, avancer que, affirmer que, montrer que). Verbs of doubting and denying take the subjunctive (contester que, douter que, il n'est pas certain que, on ne saurait dire que). Getting the mood right is how you show, in one word, whether you are reporting or questioning.

blocks.heading: Connectors for weighing a debate
blocks.body: C1 historiographical prose is built on connectors. Use certes… mais and il est vrai que… toutefois to concede before objecting; en revanche and à l'inverse to contrast; quoi qu'il en soit to close a digression; force est de constater que to admit something reluctantly. These are exactly the phrases an examiner listens for.

examples.french: Certes, la série est lacunaire ; mais elle reste la seule disponible.
examples.english: Admittedly the series has gaps; but it remains the only one available.

examples.french: Il est vrai que l'échantillon est mince ; toutefois, les résultats concordent.
examples.english: It is true that the sample is thin; nevertheless, the results agree.

examples.french: Delaunay raisonne sur les prix ; Marchand, en revanche, part des salaires.
examples.english: Delaunay reasons from prices; Marchand, on the other hand, starts from wages.

examples.french: Quoi qu'il en soit, aucune des deux lectures n'est absurde.
examples.english: Be that as it may, neither of the two readings is absurd.

examples.french: Force est de constater que le dossier n'a guère avancé depuis 1996.
examples.english: One must acknowledge that the file has hardly progressed since 1996.

examples.french: En dépit de ces réserves, l'apport du livre reste considérable.
examples.english: In spite of these reservations, the book's contribution remains considerable.

blocks.tip: Concede first, object second. A French reader expects « certes » to be followed by « mais » within the same paragraph — leaving the concession unanswered reads as agreement.

passages.title: Trois lectures de la fonderie de Vaulnes
passages.french:
Peu de dossiers illustrent aussi bien le travail historiographique que celui de la petite fonderie de Vaulnes.
En 1961, Étienne Delaunay publie une monographie fondée sur les livres de comptes conservés à la mairie.
Il y soutient que l'atelier fermait chaque hiver, faute d'eau motrice, et fait de cette saisonnalité la clef de la pauvreté du bourg.
La démonstration est élégante, les chiffres sont clairs, et la thèse fait autorité pendant vingt ans.
En 1983, Claire Marchand reprend le même fonds et objecte que les livraisons de janvier, régulières et souvent importantes, contredisent l'idée d'un arrêt complet.
Elle avance que les comptes de Delaunay enregistraient les paiements et non la production, décalage classique qui déplace tout le calendrier.
La controverse s'installe, courtoise mais réelle, et occupe plusieurs comptes rendus de revues régionales.
Le colloque de 1996 lui donne une troisième issue, plus intéressante que la victoire de l'un ou de l'autre.
Une équipe y présente les carnets d'un charretier, retrouvés dans un fonds notarial voisin et jusque-là ignorés.
Ces carnets montrent une activité réduite l'hiver, sans interruption totale, et surtout variable d'une décennie à l'autre.
Autrement dit, les deux lectures étaient exactes, mais pour des périodes différentes.
Certes, ce genre de conciliation peut sembler commode ; toutefois, elle repose ici sur une source indépendante des deux premières.
Ce que le dossier enseigne n'est pas qu'un historien avait tort, mais que chaque interprétation portait la marque des documents disponibles.
Réviser ne consiste pas à effacer Delaunay : sa monographie reste le premier travail sérieux sur la question.
Quoi qu'il en soit, l'affaire rappelle une règle simple : une thèse ne vaut jamais mieux que le corpus qui la porte.
Et un corpus, par définition, peut toujours s'agrandir.
passages.english:
Few files illustrate the work of historiography as well as that of the small foundry at Vaulnes.
In 1961, Étienne Delaunay published a monograph based on the account books kept at the town hall.
In it he maintains that the workshop closed every winter, for lack of water power, and makes this seasonality the key to the village's poverty.
The demonstration is elegant, the figures are clear, and the thesis is authoritative for twenty years.
In 1983, Claire Marchand takes up the same collection and objects that the January deliveries, regular and often substantial, contradict the idea of a complete shutdown.
She puts forward that Delaunay's accounts recorded payments rather than production, a classic discrepancy that shifts the whole calendar.
The controversy sets in, courteous but real, and fills several review sections of regional journals.
The 1996 conference gives it a third outcome, more interesting than a victory for either side.
There a team presents the notebooks of a carter, found in a neighbouring notarial collection and ignored until then.
These notebooks show reduced activity in winter, without total interruption, and above all varying from one decade to the next.
In other words, both readings were accurate, but for different periods.
Admittedly, this kind of reconciliation can seem convenient; nevertheless, it rests here on a source independent of the first two.
What the file teaches is not that one historian was wrong, but that each interpretation bore the mark of the documents available.
Revising does not consist in erasing Delaunay: his monograph remains the first serious work on the question.
Be that as it may, the case recalls a simple rule: a thesis is never worth more than the body of sources that carries it.
And a body of sources, by definition, can always grow.
